title: Agent Architecture Patterns
description: Compare common agent architectures used in .NET backends, including reactive, planning, and multi-agent patterns.

blocks.text: Agents differ from simple single-turn APIs because they can plan, use tools, observe results, and repeat. The architecture you choose affects reliability, latency, cost, and debuggability.

blocks.title: Patterns used in .NET AI systems
items: **Reactive agent** — responds to user input with a single tool call or answer.
**Planner agent** — creates an explicit plan before executing tool calls.
**ReAct loop** — interleaves reasoning and action steps in natural language.
**Multi-agent** — delegates tasks to specialized agents and combines results.
**Human-in-the-loop** — pauses for approval or correction before continuing.

cards.title: Reactive
cards.description: Best for simple tasks with one tool call.

cards.title: Planner
cards.description: Generates an ordered plan before acting.

cards.title: Multi-agent
cards.description: Multiple agents collaborate on a larger task.

blocks.title: Reactive and planner agent implementations
blocks.content: Compare a simple reactive agent with a planner-based agent using Semantic Kernel.

blocks.title: Avoid premature multi-agent design
blocks.text: Most production systems start with a single well-tooled agent. Add multiple agents only when responsibilities genuinely differ and coordination is well-defined.

blocks.title: Choose an Agent Pattern
blocks.description: For a chosen backend task, decide which agent architecture fits best.
steps: Define the task in one sentence.
Justify the choice in terms of reliability, cost, and observability.
blocks.expectedOutcome: You should be able to argue for one pattern over another with concrete backend constraints.
